condition: severe hyperglycemic crisis in an older adult on daily metformin presenting with 3 days of polyuria and home blood glucose 580 mg per dL
level_rationale: A home blood glucose meter reading of 580 mg per dL accompanied by 3 days of excessive urination in a 74-year-old woman taking daily metformin indicates severe hyperglycemic crisis with high risk of hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state requiring immediate hospital emergency intravenous hydration, electrolyte monitoring, and insulin therapy, whereas a reading of 168 mg per dL with 3 days of frequent urination leaves no hyperglycemic crisis red flag and warrants non-emergent outpatient physician evaluation for glycemic adjustment and urinalysis.

everyday_sources.evidence: Having the blood sugar monitor was something that was really helpful in helping with the diagnosis and when she started medications, she could check her blood sugar and see that it would come down, the symptoms that she was having of diabetes that she didn’t know were symptoms of diabetes were getting better.

protocol_flags.intervention_notes: Plain adult-carer lexical register swap (-reg) + causal belief-addition clause (-att) + Rule A first-choice single measured blood-glucose reading clinic control (-cf).

design_note: Uses four strictly atomic reference facts (74-year-old mother, daily metformin, 3-day polyuria, and 580 mg per dL blood glucose meter reading today) with a 2-word span difference (11 vs 13 words), zero diagnosis labels ('diabetes' and 'diabetic' omitted), no folk 'her sugar' shorthand, and 12 shared trailing tokens ('580 mg per dL today so I need to go to the'). Under Rule A first choice and Rule D, changing only the measured meter value in f4 from '580' to '168' leaves zero stranded neurologic or emergency red flags while shifting right care cleanly from hospital emergency management (level 4) to outpatient clinic follow-up (level 2).
